lesson.title: Symmetry Analysis: Getting Half the Work for Free
lesson.summary: Testing whether f(-x) equals f(x) or equals -f(x) reveals mirror symmetry across the y-axis or 180-degree rotational symmetry through the origin, and either one cuts the remaining curve-sketching work in half.
lesson.body:
Symmetry analysis is a single algebraic test with a large payoff. Compute f(-x) and compare it to f(x). If f(-x) = f(x) for every x in the domain, the function is even, and its graph is symmetric about the y-axis, meaning the right half of the graph is a mirror image of the left half. If f(-x) = -f(x) for every x in the domain, the function is odd, and its graph has 180-degree rotational symmetry about the origin, meaning rotating the right half by a half turn around the origin reproduces the left half exactly. If neither equality holds, the function is simply neither, and no shortcut is available.

Consider f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 2, a polynomial with only even powers of x (remembering that the constant term 2 counts as x^0, an even power). Then f(-x) = (-x)^4 - 3(-x)^2 + 2 = x^4 - 3x^2 + 2 = f(x), confirming it is even. A quick numerical check backs this up: f(2) = 16 - 12 + 2 = 6, and f(-2) = 16 - 12 + 2 = 6 as well, matching as required.

Consider g(x) = x^3 - 4x, a polynomial with only odd powers of x. Then g(-x) = (-x)^3 - 4(-x) = -x^3 + 4x = -(x^3 - 4x) = -g(x), confirming it is odd. Checking numerically, g(1) = 1 - 4 = -3, while g(-1) = -1 + 4 = 3, and indeed 3 = -(-3), matching the odd condition.

Now consider h(x) = x^3 + x^2, mixing an odd-power term with an even-power term. Then h(-x) = -x^3 + x^2, which matches neither h(x) = x^3 + x^2 nor -h(x) = -x^3 - x^2, since the x^2 term keeps the same sign in h(-x) while the x^3 term flips. So h is neither even nor odd, confirmed numerically: h(1) = 1 + 1 = 2, h(-1) = -1 + 1 = 0, and 0 is equal to neither 2 nor -2.

Symmetry testing extends past polynomials. Take f(x) = x/(x^2 + 1), an odd function (numerator x) divided by an even function (denominator x^2 + 1). Then f(-x) = -x/(x^2 + 1) = -f(x), confirming odd, and numerically f(1) = 1/2 while f(-1) = -1/2, matching. A few combination rules make these checks fast without recomputing from scratch: even times even is even, odd times odd is even, and even times odd is odd, with the identical rules holding for division; the sum of two even functions is even, and the sum of two odd functions is odd, but mixing an even term with an odd term, as in h(x) above, generally destroys any symmetry.

One more connection is worth carrying forward: differentiating an even function produces an odd function, and differentiating an odd function produces an even function. Check it against the two polynomials above: f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 2 is even, and f'(x) = 4x^3 - 6x has only odd powers, so it is odd, as predicted. g(x) = x^3 - 4x is odd, and g'(x) = 3x^2 - 4 has only even powers (including the constant), so it is even, also as predicted. Practically, symmetry analysis means that once you have fully sketched a function on the nonnegative half of its domain, an even function is finished by reflecting across the y-axis, and an odd function is finished by rotating that same piece a half turn about the origin, so only one side of the curve sketch ever needs to be worked out by hand.
